Georgian is a Caucasian language spoken in Georgia, remarkable for its unique writing system called Mkhedruli script, which is neither an alphabet, abjad, nor abugida but a distinct writing system of its own. The language has an ancient literary tradition stretching to the fifth century and is known for its complex consonant clusters and ergative-absolutive alignment. Georgian is a Kartvelian language with roughly 4 million native speakers primarily in Georgia and uses ergative-absolutive alignment in its grammar, rare in European languages. The language features three native writing systems: Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri, and Mkhedruli, with Mkhedruli used in modern Georgian, and each writing system developed independently and was adapted to fit the language's phonology. One of the most distinctive modern writing systems, the Mkhedruli script developed organically rather than being borrowed from another tradition. Georgian is famous for tolerating consonant clusters unusual in world languages, with clusters like gvprtskvni, which means you peel us, pronounced as a single syllabic unit. The language has rich inflectional morphology with numerous cases and a complex system of verb agreement where verbs mark person, number, tense, and mood. Georgian possesses a continuous ancient literary tradition with the oldest texts dating to the fifth century in the form of hagiographies, and the language became a literary vehicle for Christian Orthodoxy in the Caucasus. While linguistically somewhat isolated, Georgian's relationship to other Caucasian language families remains disputed, though some scholars group it with other Kartvelian languages within the larger Caucasian language family, one of the most linguistically complex in the world.
